title: Albondigas en Salsa
subtitle: Spanish meatballs in tomato and white wine sauce
excerpt: Albondigas are Spanish meatballs: a mix of pork and beef mince seasoned with garlic, parsley, and egg, fried until golden, and then simmered in a simple tomato and white wine sauce. They are one of the most popular tapas dishes in Spain and also a classic family dinner served with rice or crusty bread.
sourceNotes: Albondigas are found across Spain and Latin America, and appear in the medieval cookbook Ruperto de Nola's Libre de Coch (1520). The word comes from the Arabic al-bunduq (hazelnut), referring to the round shape. Spanish albondigas differ from Italian meatballs in being lighter and usually finished in a tomato-wine sauce.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in their sauce. Reheat gently.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made a day ahead.

content.text: Spanish meatballs are smaller than Italian ones -- about the size of a walnut. Frying them first gives a brown crust that holds the ball together during the sauce simmer. Do not skip the fry: meatballs dropped raw into sauce fall apart. Rest the formed balls in the fridge for 15 minutes before frying if the mixture feels soft.

Combine {{beef-mince}} beef mince, {{pork-mince}} pork mince, {{breadcrumbs-dried}} breadcrumbs, grated {{garlic}} garlic, {{parsley-flat}} parsley, {{eggs}} egg, {{salt-table}} salt, and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Mix well. Roll into walnut-sized balls and dust in {{plain-flour}} flour.
Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Brown the meatballs on all sides in batches, about 4 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} onion to the pan and cook for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} garlic and {{smoked-paprika}} smoked paprika. Cook for 1 minute. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} wine and simmer for 2 minutes. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} tomatoes and simmer for 10 minutes.
Return the meatballs to the pan. Cover and simmer for 15 minutes until cooked through. Taste for {{salt-table}} salt. Serve with crusty bread or rice.

items.symptom: The meatballs broke apart during frying
items.cause: The mixture was too warm and soft when rolled, or too little egg was used.
items.fix: Refrigerate the formed balls for 15 minutes before frying. Handle them gently -- turn once only during browning. A cold, firm ball holds together much better.

content.text: Albondigas appear in Spanish cooking from the medieval period. They are eaten across the whole country as both a tapas dish and a family meal. In Madrid and Barcelona they are on every tapas menu. In Mexico and across Latin America, versions in spiced tomato sauces are just as common. The dish spread with Spanish settlement and changed in every country it reached.
